newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: China, trading partners see advance to WTO entry.
newsitem.headline: China, trading partners see advance to WTO entry.

text.p: Chinese and Western negotiators said on Thursday they had made good progress towards an agreement on Beijing's admission to the World Trade Organisation (WTO) but warned more barriers lay ahead.

They were speaking after nearly two weeks of talks aimed at putting new impetus into the negotiations launched 10 years ago and largely stalled because of China's reluctance to move quickly to open up its domestic market.

"This round has been extremely positive and constructive, and has yielded important progress," China's assistant foreign trade minister Long Yongtu told a news conference after a formal session of the WTO working party preparing an entry accord.
China now saw "light at the end of the tunnel," he said.

"We clearly made some substantive progress," Lee Sands, assistant United States trade representative for East Asia, told reporters. "China is evidencing a greater understanding of the requirements of the WTO."

Pierre-Louis Girard, Swiss chairman of the working party, said three days of informal discussions involving many WTO members this week had brought "significant progress....on major issues" and indicated another round would be held in May.

Long and Western trade envoys said the main advance was a decision by China that as part of a final accord it would allow any company, Chinese or foreign, established in the country to engage in import and export trade.

The new rule, for which special legislation would be prepared, would come into effect at the end of a three-year transition period following China's admission to the WTO, Long told the news conference.

This, a major departure from the old, rigidly state-controlled Chinese foreign trade system, had been a major demand of the European Union and the United States who argued "trading rights" were vital to underpin other reforms in China.

Long said China had already gone a long way in this direction in recent years under policies introduced by late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, increasing the number of Chinese firms licensed for foreign trade from 18 in 1978 to some 12,000 today.
"But many members of the WTO had insisted that full trading rights were the cornerstone of the whole negotiation," he said.

Removing state control of foreign trade, Long declared, was "a big challenge to China" but the country was ready to face it. The decision to follow that path showed Beijing's determination to pursue Deng's opening to the outside world.

However, despite the advance, Long said he recognised there were still "many pending issues" in the negotiations -- which when completed would bring the huge Chinese market under the open trading rules of the increasingly influential trade body.

"We have come some way this week, but there is still a way to go before we can say the end is in sight," said one WTO ambassador. "Realistically, I can't see them coming in before the start of next year at the earliest."
Long himself declined to predict when entry might come. "It doesn't just depend on China," he said.
But he said Beijing was confident that remaining problems could be resolved "because we have seen a general consensus that China's early accession is in the interest of all WTO members.
"We have finally seen the light at the end of the tunnel and the light is becoming even brighter," he declared.
